736.title: Soften around it
736.hook: pain researchers describe pain as both sensation and emotion; fear and attention can change how much it hurts, and mindfulness courses help some people
736.howItsDone: Some pain clinics and hospitals offer mindfulness-based courses, and pain psychologists help people notice and loosen the fear and bracing around long-term pain, alongside medical care.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was no ranking: Job's friends sitting in silence, and pain that fills a person whatever its size. Your line was weep with them that weep.

A stubbed toe at the end of a great day: a yelp, a laugh, forgotten in a minute. The same stubbed toe at the end of a terrible day: it's the last straw, and it throbs for an hour. Same toe. Same doorframe. Something besides the toe is deciding how much it hurts. After days of scripture, novels and memoirs, this path turns to the lab and the clinic, which have their own careful things to say.
screen: `A STUBBED TOE ON A GOOD DAY.` → `THE SAME TOE ON A BAD ONE.` → `WHAT ELSE DECIDES THE HURT?`

segments.voice: First, what pain is. The International Association for the Study of Pain, a body of pain researchers and clinicians, defines pain as an unpleasant sensory and emotional experience. Both words matter. Pain is real in the body, and it's also shaped by what's going on in the mind. That doesn't mean it's imagined. It means it's whole-person. Second, fear. Pain researchers describe a loop, sometimes called the fear-avoidance model: a person in pain fears it, braces against it, moves less, watches for it, and for some people that loop keeps the pain going and makes it worse. Tensing around an ache can feed it. Third, attention. The psychologist William James wrote: "My experience is what I agree to attend to." Pain grabs attention, and attention can feed pain. But attention can also be placed differently: not away from the pain, not clenched around it, but softer and wider. Fourth, what mindfulness courses can and can't do. Programs such as Jon Kabat-Zinn's mindfulness-based stress reduction, which he says draws on Buddhist meditation, teach people with long-term pain to notice the sensation itself, without the bracing and the story. In some studies, people in these courses report that their pain bothers them less, and some report less pain. Not everyone. It isn't a cure, and the science never says the pain was all in someone's head. It says something smaller and useful: the fear and the clench around an ache are part of the hurt, and for some people, those parts can soften.
screen: `PAIN: SENSATION AND EMOTION.` · `THE FEAR LOOP.` · `WHERE ATTENTION GOES.` · `NOT A CURE. A SOFTER GRIP.` · then, large: `SOFTEN AROUND IT.`

segments.voice: Find one mild ache, a stiff neck, a tired back, a sore foot; if an ache is new or severe, that's for a doctor, not a sit. Let your attention rest near it and notice what's around it, muscles bracing, breath held, a face tensed, and on each out-breath let one of those soften a little. You're not making the ache go away, just loosening the grip around it.
Soften around it. Pain is sensation and emotion; fear and bracing can feed it, and loosening the grip helps some people. Today's word.
Your line: soften around it. The ache may stay; for some, the clench around it eases. See you tomorrow.

737.title: Growth isn't required
737.hook: some people report growth after trauma and some don't, and no one owes a silver lining
737.howItsDone: Psychologists who study posttraumatic growth describe it as something some people report after a struggle, not a requirement; Jews and Christians keep Psalm 88, a prayer that ends in darkness, in their scriptures.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was soften around it: the fear and the clench we add around pain, and how loosening the grip helps some people.

A card arrives after a hard year. On the front, in curly gold letters: everything happens for a reason. Someone meant it kindly. Still, a line like that can land like homework. Find the reason. Write up the lesson. Show your growth by Friday. Two psychologists studied what happens to people after terrible events, and what they found is more honest than the card. Some people do grow. Some don't. And the card leaves out the most important part: growth isn't required.
screen: `EVERYTHING HAPPENS FOR A REASON.` → `IT CAN LAND LIKE HOMEWORK.` → `GROWTH ISN'T REQUIRED.`

segments.voice: First, the name. Richard Tedeschi and Lawrence Calhoun, psychologists who studied people after trauma, gave one pattern a name: posttraumatic growth. Some of the people they studied described changes on the far side of the struggle. Closer relationships. New priorities. A sense of their own strength. A deeper spiritual life. Second, the fine print. In their account, the growth comes out of the struggle with what happened, not out of the event itself. The disaster isn't the teacher. And growth and distress can sit side by side: a person can report real growth and still hurt. Third, not everyone reports it. Their work describes growth as something some people find, not a stage everyone reaches, and not a test anyone passes or fails. Nobody owes the world a silver lining. Fourth, an old text that makes room for this. Earlier this year, this path read Psalm thirteen, a complaint that turns toward trust by its last verse. Psalm eighty-eight doesn't turn. It's a prayer from the bottom, and its last line in the King James Bible is this: "Lover and friend hast thou put far from me, and mine acquaintance into darkness." That's where it stops. No lesson, no bright side. And it sits in the Bible of Jews and Christians alike, ending and all. Some readers take comfort in exactly that: a holy book that lets a sufferer end in the dark without being told to cheer up. Growth may come, quietly, later on. Or it may not. Either way, the hard thing doesn't have to earn its keep.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one hard thing, past or present, not the hardest. If the mind rushes to ask what it taught you, let that question sit down: it happened, it hurt, and that's enough to say. If you pray, you can offer it with no moral attached; if a lesson shows up on its own, let it come, just don't go digging for one.

Your line: that sounds hard. Sometimes those three words are the whole kindness. Go gently.

738.title: Help is strength
738.hook: depression and trauma are not spiritual failures, and professional help is part of the path
738.howItsDone: Some religious communities encourage people facing depression or trauma to see a doctor or counselor alongside prayer or meditation, and some congregations keep lists of local counselors and crisis lines.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was posttraumatic growth. Your line was that sounds hard: growth isn't required, and a psalm can end in the dark.

The prophet Elijah is running for his life. He goes a day's journey into the wilderness, sits down under a juniper tree, and asks to die. In the King James Bible he says: "It is enough; now, O LORD, take away my life." Then he lies down and falls asleep. Some readers today hear in that scene something a doctor would take seriously: exhaustion, fear, despair, a person at the end of himself. And this is a prophet, a man of God. What happens next is today's lesson.
screen: `ELIJAH UNDER THE JUNIPER TREE.` → `IT IS ENOUGH.` → `WHAT HAPPENS NEXT?`

segments.voice: First, what the angel does. Not a sermon. The text says an angel touched him and said, "Arise and eat." There's a cake baked on the coals and a jar of water by his head. He eats, drinks, sleeps again, and the angel comes back and feeds him a second time. Care for the body comes before any word about his calling. Second, what the sciences say. Depression, and the long shadow trauma can leave, are health conditions. Doctors, psychologists and counselors study them and treat them. They aren't proof of weak faith, a bad practice, or not trying hard enough. Prayer, meditation and community can sit alongside treatment; they don't have to replace it. Third, the traditions have said something like this in their own words. The book of Sirach, part of the Bible for Catholic and Orthodox Christians, tells its readers to honor the physician, because the Lord created him. In a hadith collected by Abu Dawud, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, tells people to seek treatment, because God has not made a disease without making a remedy for it. Fourth, the strength part. Elijah doesn't fix himself under that tree. Someone touches him, feeds him, lets him sleep, and he takes it. Asking for help takes courage. Calling a doctor, a counselor, or a crisis line isn't a step off the path. For some people, it's the next step on it.
screen: `ARISE AND EAT.` · `A HEALTH CONDITION, NOT A FAILURE.` · `HONOR THE PHYSICIAN.` · `ASKING TAKES COURAGE.` · then, large: `HELP IS STRENGTH.`

segments.voice: Save one support number in your phone now: your doctor, a counselor, a crisis line where you live, or a friend who always picks up, under a plain name you'll find on a bad night. Then put the phone down, breathe, and let your hands rest knowing it's there; if you pray, you can pray for the people who answer those phones. And if you're in danger right now, stop and call your local emergency number.
Elijah, fed and let sleep by an angel under the juniper tree before any word about his calling. Today's word.
Your line: arise and eat. Even a prophet was fed before he was told anything. Day seven hundred thirty-eight, done.

739.title: Breathing in pain
739.hook: a Tibetan Buddhist practice: breathe in others' pain, breathe out relief, gently and never forced
739.carry: in with pain, out with relief
739.howItsDone: Tibetan Buddhists practice tonglen as part of lojong, or mind training, breathing in suffering and breathing out relief; teachers suggest beginning with their own pain or a loved one.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Elijah, fed under the juniper tree before he was told anything. Your line was arise and eat.

Breathe in calm, breathe out stress. That's the usual instruction in a breathing exercise. A practice from Tibetan Buddhism turns it around on purpose. Breathe in someone's pain. Breathe out relief, toward them. It sounds backwards. It even sounds a little risky, like inviting a cold into the house. And yet Tibetan teachers have taught it for a long time as a way to grow compassion. Its name is today's word, and how the teachers handle it matters as much as the practice itself.
screen: `BREATHE IN CALM, BREATHE OUT STRESS?` → `TURNED AROUND ON PURPOSE.` → `IT SOUNDS BACKWARDS.`

segments.voice: First, the name. Tonglen is Tibetan for sending and taking. On the in-breath you take in the suffering of someone, and on the out-breath you send them whatever relief you'd wish for them: warmth, ease, rest. Second, where it lives. Tonglen belongs to a Tibetan Buddhist training called lojong, which means mind training. Tradition traces it to the Indian teacher Atisha, and later teachers gathered it into short slogans meant to be carried through an ordinary day. One of them, in plain paraphrase, says to practice sending and taking in turn, riding them on the breath. Third, why it runs this way. A mind tends to pull away from pain and reach for comfort. Tonglen reverses that habit on purpose, as a way of opening the heart instead of closing it. Teachers present it as a training in compassion, not as magic that moves someone's illness into your body. Fourth, gently. Pema Chödrön, a modern teacher in this lineage, suggests starting close: with your own pain, or with one person you love, before anyone harder. And the practice widens from there: whoever else is hurting the same way. Two words carry the whole method: never forced. Tonglen isn't a test of how much pain a person can swallow. It's a few honest breaths in the direction of someone else.
screen: `TONGLEN: SENDING AND TAKING.` · `PART OF LOJONG, MIND TRAINING.` · `IT REVERSES THE HABIT OF PULLING AWAY.` · `START CLOSE, AND GENTLY.` · then, large: `IN WITH PAIN, OUT WITH RELIEF.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person you care about who's struggling. For three breaths, breathe in a little of their heaviness, like warm, dark air, only as much as feels okay, and breathe out ease toward them, like cool, clear light; then simply breathe. If it feels like too much, come back to your own breath, which is part of the practice too, and if you pray, you can hold their name.
Tonglen: Tibetan, sending and taking. Breathe in someone's pain, breathe out relief, gently and never forced. Today's word.
Your line: in with pain, out with relief. Start close, and let the circle widen in its own time. That's day seven hundred thirty-nine.

740.title: Your own lament
740.hook: write a lament the way the psalmists did
740.howItsDone: Jews and Christians pray and read the laments of the Bible, including David's lament for Saul and Jonathan and the psalms of complaint, and some write laments of their own in grief.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was tonglen, sending and taking on the breath. Your line was in with pain, out with relief.

A man comes to David with his clothes torn and earth on his head. He brings news from the battle. Saul, the king, is dead. So is Jonathan, Saul's son, David's friend. David doesn't make a speech about God's plan. The text says he tears his clothes, mourns, weeps, and fasts until evening. And then he does something else. He puts the grief into words. The Bible calls it a lamentation, and it's today's model.
screen: `NEWS FROM THE BATTLE.` → `DAVID TEARS HIS CLOTHES AND WEEPS.` → `THEN HE PUTS IT INTO WORDS.`

segments.voice: Four things in David's lament, and anyone can borrow them. First, it's specific. It names names: Saul and Jonathan. It names the place: the mountains of Gilboa, where they fell. It doesn't melt grief into a general mood. Second, it has a refrain. The lament keeps coming back to the same cry, in the King James words: "How are the mighty fallen!" A refrain gives grief somewhere to return when the other words run out. In between, David asks that the news not be told in the enemy's towns, so no one there can rejoice over it. Third, it says what was good. Of Jonathan, David says: "very pleasant hast thou been unto me: thy love to me was wonderful, passing the love of women." A lament doesn't only count the loss. It holds up what was lost, and it honors Saul as well as Jonathan. Fourth, it doesn't fix anything. No lesson is tacked on at the end. The last line returns to the refrain: "How are the mighty fallen, and the weapons of war perished!" The grief is allowed to stay grief. A lament isn't a complaint letter and it isn't a eulogy. It's grief with a shape, honest enough to name what hurts and loving enough to name what was good.
screen: `IT NAMES NAMES AND PLACES.` · `IT HAS A REFRAIN.` · `IT SAYS WHAT WAS GOOD.` · `IT DOESN'T FIX ANYTHING.` · then, large: `HOW ARE THE MIGHTY FALLEN!`

segments.voice: On paper or a phone note, write six lines about one loss or hard thing: name it, what was good, what's gone, what hurts now, what you'd ask for if you could, and one short refrain to come back to. It doesn't have to be poetry, and it doesn't have to be addressed to anyone; if you pray, you can address it to God, the way the psalmists did.
Qinah, Hebrew for a lament, the shape David gave his grief for Saul and Jonathan: specific, honest, and unfixed. Today's word.
Your line: my lament. Six honest lines are yours to keep, shown to no one. Day seven hundred forty, done.

741.title: Less advice
741.carry: swift to hear, slow to speak
741.howItsDone: Hospital and hospice chaplains of different traditions are trained in listening, and some Christians recall James 1:19, swift to hear, slow to speak, when they sit with those who are struggling.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was qinah, David's lament for Saul and Jonathan. Your line was my lament: grief with a shape.

My mom's back in the hospital. Six words, and before they've finished landing, the suggestions arrive. Have you tried a second opinion? You need to take a week off. My cousin had the same thing, and she did this. Every one of them kind. Hardly any of them asked for. The person who said those six words is still standing there, now holding a small pile of homework on top of the worry. Today: the urge to fix, and what happens when it waits.
screen: `MY MOM'S BACK IN THE HOSPITAL.` → `THE SUGGESTIONS ARRIVE.` → `KIND, AND NOT ASKED FOR.`

segments.voice: First, Job, briefly. After chapter upon chapter of his friends' explanations, Job's verdict on all that talk, in the King James Bible, is short: "miserable comforters are ye all." Every answer they gave was meant to help. None of it comforted him. Second, James. The letter of James puts the order of things in one line: "let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak." Notice the order. Hearing comes first, and fast. Speaking comes second, and slowly. A ready answer is the fast part, and the letter asks for it to be the slow one. Third, Ecclesiastes, the book that lists the seasons of a life, gives "a time to keep silence, and a time to speak." In that line, silence comes first. Fourth, why this works, even outside scripture. Advice, even good advice, can quietly tell a hurting person they're a problem to be solved. Presence tells them they're a person worth staying with. Some chaplains and counselors use a simple question before offering anything: do you want ideas, or do you want me to listen? Then they take the answer seriously. Sometimes the answer is ideas, and then advice is a gift. But asked first, it lands as care instead of correction.
screen: `MISERABLE COMFORTERS ARE YE ALL.` · `SWIFT TO HEAR, SLOW TO SPEAK.` · `A TIME TO KEEP SILENCE.` · `IDEAS, OR LISTENING?` · then, large: `LESS ADVICE.`

segments.voice: Picture sitting beside someone who's having a hard time as they start to talk. Notice the urge to fix rise, in the chest or on the tongue, and let it pass like a car going by; say only, that sounds hard, tell me more, and stay with them in the quiet. If you pray, you can hold them there too.
Less advice. Presence before solutions: swift to hear, slow to speak, and a time to keep silence. Today's word.
Your line: swift to hear, slow to speak. Listening first is a kind of help, too. See you tomorrow.

742.title: This is hard
742.hook: Kristin Neff's practice: hand on heart, "this is hard, others feel this too"
742.howItsDone: Kristin Neff teaches a short self-compassion break: noticing a moment of suffering, remembering that others feel it too, and offering oneself kindness, sometimes with a hand on the heart.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was less advice. Your line was swift to hear, slow to speak: presence before solutions.

A friend in pain gets patience and a gentle voice. The inner voice, on a bad day, can sound more like a drill sergeant. So what about when the one who's hurting is you? The psychologist Kristin Neff, who studies self-compassion, built a practice for that moment. It takes one hand and a few plain words, and it's small enough to do in a parked car.
screen: `THE INNER DRILL SERGEANT.` → `WHAT IF THE ONE HURTING IS YOU?` → `ONE HAND, A FEW PLAIN WORDS.`

segments.voice: First, three parts. Neff describes self-compassion as having three pieces. Mindfulness: noticing that this is a moment of suffering, without blowing it up or brushing it off. Common humanity: remembering that suffering is part of being human. Not, others have it worse. Others feel this too. And kindness: treating yourself the way you'd treat a friend who was hurting. Second, the short version. In what she calls a self-compassion break, those three pieces become three plain moves. Something like: this is hard. Others feel this too. And a wish to be kind to yourself, in whatever words fit. People choose their own words. The three moves matter more than a script. Third, the hand. Neff suggests a soothing touch, a hand on the heart or wherever feels comforting, as a way of telling the body what the words are telling the mind. Fourth, the week. It began in the lab and the clinic: soften around it, posttraumatic growth, Elijah. Then it turned to practices for hard days: tonglen, qinah, less advice. Several of those point outward, toward someone else's pain. Today turns the same care inward. Less advice and more presence works on the inside, too.
screen: `THREE PARTS OF SELF-COMPASSION.` · `THIS IS HARD. OTHERS FEEL THIS TOO.` · `A HAND ON THE HEART.` · `THE WEEK'S CARE, TURNED INWARD.` · then, large: `THIS IS HARD.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something mildly hard from today and, if it feels okay, place a hand on your heart or wherever is comforting. Quietly, in your own words: this is hard; others feel this too; and one kind wish for yourself. Then let the hand rest or drop, and just breathe; if you pray, you can bring the same three moves to God.
Kristin Neff, the psychologist whose self-compassion break pairs noticing, common humanity, and kindness toward yourself. Today's word.
Your line: others feel this too. The care you'd give a friend has room for you as well. Day seven hundred forty-two.
